guide.summary: Unit 3 covers how populations grow and are limited, then applies those ideas to humans: generalists vs. specialists, r- and K-selected species, survivorship curves, carrying capacity, age-structure diagrams, total fertility rate, growth-rate and doubling-time calculations, and the demographic transition. Calculations from this unit appear on nearly every exam.

sections.heading: Life history strategies
sections.body: Specialists have narrow niches (specific food or habitat) and are vulnerable to change; generalists have broad niches and tolerate disturbance, which is why many invasive species are generalists. r-selected species produce many offspring with little parental care, mature quickly, and boom and bust (insects, weeds); K-selected species produce few offspring with high parental care, mature slowly, and stay near carrying capacity (elephants, whales), so they recover slowly from declines. Survivorship curves: Type I, high survival until old age (large mammals); Type II, constant mortality (some birds, rodents); Type III, very high early mortality (fish, plants, oysters).

sections.heading: Population growth and limits
sections.body: With unlimited resources, populations grow exponentially (J-curve). Limited resources produce logistic growth (S-curve) that levels off at carrying capacity (K). A population can overshoot K and then die back as resources are depleted. Density-dependent factors (food, disease, competition, predation) intensify as density rises; density-independent factors (drought, fire, hurricanes, freezes) affect a population regardless of density.

sections.heading: Human population calculations
sections.body: Growth rate (%) = (crude birth rate − crude death rate) ÷ 10, when rates are per 1,000. Including migration: change = (births + immigration) − (deaths + emigration); percent change = change ÷ initial population × 100. Rule of 70: doubling time (years) ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate (%). Total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children per woman; replacement level is about 2.1 in developed countries (higher where child mortality is high). TFR falls with women's education and employment, access to family planning, lower infant mortality, and urbanization.

sections.heading: Age structure and demographic transition
sections.body: Age-structure diagrams with a wide base (pyramid) indicate rapid growth; straight sides (column) indicate stability; a narrow base (inverted) indicates decline and an aging population with fewer workers per retiree. Population momentum: even after TFR drops to replacement, a population keeps growing for decades because many young people are entering reproductive age. Demographic transition: Stage 1, high birth and death rates (preindustrial). Stage 2, death rates fall (sanitation, medicine, food) while birth rates stay high, so growth is fastest. Stage 3, birth rates fall (industrializing). Stage 4, both are low (industrial). Some countries enter a fifth stage of decline.

keyTakeaways: K-selected species recover slowly; r-selected recover quickly.
Wide-base pyramid → rapid growth; narrow base → decline.
Stage 2 of the demographic transition has the fastest growth.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to divide (CBR − CDR) by 10 when rates are per 1,000.
Using 70 ÷ 0.02 instead of 70 ÷ 2 for a 2% rate.
Confusing Type I and Type III survivorship.
Thinking a population stops growing the moment TFR hits replacement.
examTips: Show the formula with numbers for every calculation; FRQ points require the setup.
Age-structure diagrams are common stimuli; read the bars for 0–14 and 65+.
Demographic transition questions ask which stage fits given birth and death rates.
Link TFR changes to specific causes (education, contraception, economics).
guide.cramSheet:
**Strategies:** r = many, fast, no care · K = few, slow, care · specialist vs. generalist

**Survivorship:** I old-age deaths · II constant · III early deaths

**Growth:** J exponential · S logistic → K · overshoot → dieback

**Factors:** density-dependent (food, disease) · independent (weather, fire)

**Math:** r% = (CBR − CDR)/10 · Δ = (B + I) − (D + E) · t₂ = 70/r%

**TFR:** replacement ≈ 2.1 · ↓ with education, family planning

**DTM:** 1 high/high · 2 deaths ↓ · 3 births ↓ · 4 low/low

vocab.definition: A species with a narrow niche and specific needs.
A species with a broad niche that tolerates varied conditions.

Species with few offspring, extensive parental care, and slow maturity.
A graph showing the proportion of a cohort surviving at each age.
The maximum population an environment can sustain over time.
When a population temporarily exceeds carrying capacity, often followed by dieback.
A limiting factor whose effect increases with population density.

practice.stem: A sea turtle lays about 100 eggs per nest, and most hatchlings are eaten within days. Which survivorship curve fits this species?
practice.explanation: High mortality early in life, with few survivors reaching adulthood, is Type III.

practice.stem: A country's population grows at 2% per year. Its approximate doubling time is
Which species is most likely to be harmed by the loss of a single plant species?

choices.text: A raccoon that eats fruit, insects, eggs, and garbage
A caterpillar that feeds only on one species of milkweed
A coyote that hunts small mammals and scavenges
A crow that eats seeds, insects, and carrion

practice.explanation: A specialist with a single food source cannot switch when that resource disappears.

practice.stem: An age-structure diagram with a very wide base that narrows sharply toward the top indicates a population that is
practice.explanation: A large proportion of children means many future parents; growth will continue.

practice.stem: A country has a crude birth rate of 30 per 1,000 and a crude death rate of 10 per 1,000, with no net migration. What are its growth rate and doubling time?

distractors.A: Forgets that rates are per 1,000, not per 100.

practice.stimulus: Twenty-five deer are introduced to an island with no predators. The population grows to 1,800 in 20 years, then crashes to 50 within three years as vegetation is stripped.

choices.text: logistic growth leveling at carrying capacity
overshoot of carrying capacity followed by dieback

practice.explanation: The population exceeded what the vegetation could sustain, degraded its resource base, and collapsed.

distractors.A: Logistic growth levels off rather than crashing.

practice.stem: Replacement-level fertility is higher in countries with high infant mortality than in countries with low infant mortality because

choices.text: more children must be born to ensure two survive to reproductive age
families in those countries prefer larger families
immigration is higher in those countries
life expectancy is longer in those countries

practice.explanation: Replacement means each couple is replaced by two adults; higher child mortality raises the births needed.

distractors.B: Preference affects actual TFR, not replacement level.

practice.stem: A country's death rate has fallen sharply due to improved sanitation and vaccines, while its birth rate remains high. It is in which stage of the demographic transition?
practice.explanation: Stage 2: falling death rates with high birth rates produce the fastest growth.

distractors.C: Stage 3 begins when birth rates start falling.

practice.stem: A town of 50,000 people has 800 births, 500 deaths, 300 immigrants, and 100 emigrants in one year. What is its percent growth that year?
Which policy has been most consistently associated with a decline in total fertility rate?

choices.text: Increasing educational opportunities for girls and women
Providing tax credits for each additional child
Lowering the minimum age of marriage

practice.explanation: Education delays marriage, increases workforce participation, and improves knowledge of family planning.

practice.stem: A country's TFR fell to 2.1 ten years ago, but its population is projected to grow for another 40 years. Which explains this?

choices.text: A large cohort born when TFR was high is now entering reproductive age, so total births stay high even at replacement fertility.
TFR does not affect population size.

practice.explanation: Population momentum: many parents × 2.1 children each still yields many births.

practice.stimulus: Country P: 13% of the population is under 15 and 29% is over 65. TFR is 1.3.
practice.stem: Which challenge is Country P most likely to face?

choices.text: A shrinking workforce supporting a growing number of retirees
A shortage of schools for a rapidly growing number of children
Rapid population growth straining food supply

practice.explanation: A narrow base and large elderly share mean fewer working-age people per retiree, stressing pensions and health care.

practice.stem: Which factor would limit a rabbit population regardless of its density?

choices.text: A viral disease spread by contact
An unusually late spring frost that kills young rabbits
Increased predation by foxes attracted to abundant prey

practice.explanation: Weather events are density-independent: they kill a similar proportion whatever the population size.

distractors.A: Disease spreads faster at high density.

practice.stem: A country of 8.0 million people grows at a constant 3.5% per year. Approximately what will its population be in 40 years?
practice.explanation: Doubling time = 70/3.5 = 20 years; 40 years = 2 doublings: 8 → 16 → 32 million.

practice.frqType: Q3 Analyze an Environmental Problem and Propose a Solution Doing Calculations
practice.prompt: Country Z had a population of 40 million in 2020. Its crude birth rate is 28 per 1,000, its crude death rate is 8 per 1,000, and net migration is zero. About 42% of its population is under age 15. Most of its population works in agriculture, and its cities are growing quickly.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate Country Z's annual growth rate as a percent. Show your work.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the doubling time of the population. Show your work.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Assuming the growth rate stays constant, calculate the population in 2090. Show your work.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Identify the stage of the demographic transition Country Z is most likely in, and justify your answer with the data.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Describe the shape of Country Z's age-structure diagram.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Propose one strategy that would reduce Country Z's total fertility rate, and explain how it would work.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Describe one environmental problem likely to result from rapid urban growth in Country Z.

rubric.description: Death rate is low (8) but birth rate remains high (28), producing rapid growth.
Pyramid: wide base of young people narrowing toward older ages.
E.g., expand girls' education, provide access to contraception, improve child health care, offer economic opportunities for women.
E.g., education delays marriage and first births and increases women's economic opportunities, lowering desired family size.
E.g., air pollution from traffic and industry, inadequate sewage treatment contaminating water, loss of farmland and habitat to sprawl, urban heat island.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Growth rate = (28 − 8)/1,000 = 20/1,000 = 0.020 = 2.0% per year.

(b) Doubling time = 70 ÷ 2.0 = 35 years.

(c) 2020 to 2090 is 70 years, or 70/35 = 2 doublings. 40 million × 2 × 2 = 160 million.

(d) Stage 2. The death rate (8 per 1,000) is already low, but the birth rate (28 per 1,000) remains high, so the population grows rapidly, as in Stage 2.

(e) A pyramid with a wide base, because 42% of the population is under 15, narrowing toward the older age groups.

(f) Expand secondary education for girls. Women who stay in school longer tend to marry later, start families later, and have more job opportunities, so they choose to have fewer children.

(g) Rapidly growing cities may lack adequate sewage treatment, so untreated waste enters rivers, contaminating drinking water and spreading waterborne disease.
